title: Public Health Fundamentals
summary: Learn how public health protects populations: measuring disease with epidemiology, how infections spread and are controlled, screening and vaccination, water, nutrition and environment, and health systems and promotion.
audience: Health students, community health workers, NGO staff and anyone interested in population health

body.p: Public health is the science and practice of protecting and improving the health of whole populations, rather than treating one patient at a time. It works through prevention: clean water, vaccination, safe food, health education, disease surveillance, road safety and policies such as tobacco taxes.

list: Biology and genetics.
Behaviours: diet, physical activity, smoking, alcohol, sexual health.
Living and working conditions: housing, water, sanitation, air quality, workplace safety.
Social and economic factors: income, education, employment, gender and discrimination.
Access to quality health services.

body.p: Many of the biggest gains in life expectancy came from public-health measures rather than hospitals: safe water and sewers, vaccines, better nutrition and safer childbirth. Today countries face a double burden of infectious diseases (such as malaria, TB and HIV) and non-communicable diseases (such as hypertension, diabetes and cancers).

body.tip: When you hear about a health problem, ask who is most affected and why; the answer usually points to the causes public health can tackle.

body.p: Epidemiology studies how often diseases occur, in whom, where and when, and why. Counts alone mislead because populations differ in size, so we use rates.

list: Incidence: new cases in a period. 250 new cases in a district of 500 000 people in a year is 250 / 500 000 x 100 000 = 50 per 100 000 per year.
Prevalence: everyone who has the condition at a point in time, new or old.
Case fatality rate: deaths among cases. 12 deaths among 400 cases is 3%.
Rates per 1000: 1200 births in a population of 40 000 is a crude birth rate of 30 per 1000.
Descriptive studies show patterns by person, place and time.
Case-control studies compare people with and without a disease to find past exposures.
Cohort studies follow groups over time to see who develops disease.
Randomised controlled trials test interventions such as vaccines and medicines.

body.p: Association is not causation: confounding factors can link an exposure and a disease. Strong, consistent findings across good studies, with a plausible mechanism, build the case for cause.

body.tip: Always check the denominator: "500 cases" means little until you know out of how many people and over what time.

lessons.title: How infections spread and how to stop them

body.p: Infectious diseases spread through routes such as air and droplets (TB, measles, influenza), contaminated water and food (cholera, typhoid), insect vectors (malaria, dengue), blood and sexual contact (HIV, hepatitis B) and direct contact. Breaking any link in the chain of infection (agent, reservoir, way out, route, way in, susceptible host) can stop spread.

R₀ is the average number of people one case infects in a fully susceptible population. If R₀ is above 1 the outbreak grows; below 1 it shrinks. Herd immunity is reached when the immune share exceeds 1 - 1/R₀: for R₀ = 4, 1 - 1/4 = 75%; for a very contagious disease such as measles with R₀ around 15, about 93%, which is why very high vaccine coverage is needed.

list: Vaccination protects individuals and, at high coverage, whole communities.
Hand washing with soap, safe water and sanitation stop faecal-oral diseases.
Insecticide-treated nets and removing standing water reduce malaria.
Early diagnosis, treatment and contact tracing reduce TB and other spread.
Surveillance detects outbreaks early so they can be contained.

body.tip: Hand washing with soap at key times (after the toilet, before eating or preparing food) is one of the cheapest life-saving habits there is.

body.p: Screening tests apparently healthy people to find disease early, such as blood-pressure checks, cervical cancer screening and newborn tests. A good screening programme targets an important condition with an accurate, acceptable test and an effective treatment.

list: Sensitivity: the share of people with the disease who test positive.
Specificity: the share of people without the disease who test negative.
Positive predictive value (PPV): the share of positive results that are true positives.

body.p: Example: screen 10 000 people where 2% (200) have a disease, using a test with 95% sensitivity and 90% specificity. True positives = 190. False positives = 10% of the 9800 without the disease = 980. PPV = 190 / (190 + 980), only about 16.2%. When a disease is rare, most positives are false alarms, so positive screening results need confirmation tests. The negative predictive value here is about 99.9%, so a negative result is very reassuring.

National immunisation schedules protect children against diseases such as measles, polio, diphtheria, whooping cough and pneumonia. Programmes track coverage, keep vaccines in the cold chain and respond to rumours with clear, trusted information.

body.tip: Explain screening results with natural frequencies ("of every 1000 people tested…"); people understand them far better than percentages.

body.p: Unsafe water, poor sanitation and lack of hygiene cause diarrhoeal diseases that still kill many young children. Safely managed water, toilets that separate waste from people, and hand washing are basic public-health foundations.

list: Undernutrition in children shows as stunting (low height for age) and wasting (low weight for height).
Micronutrient deficiencies, such as iron, vitamin A and iodine, harm growth, learning and immunity; fortifying foods such as salt and flour helps whole populations.
Exclusive breastfeeding for about the first six months protects infants.
Diets high in processed foods, sugar and salt contribute to rising obesity, diabetes and hypertension.
Indoor smoke from cooking with wood or charcoal harms lungs; cleaner stoves and fuels help.
Outdoor air pollution, extreme heat and flooding are growing risks.
Road traffic injuries are a leading cause of death for young people; helmets, seatbelts and speed limits save lives.

body.tip: Public-health action often happens outside the health sector: water engineers, teachers, planners and road-safety officers all prevent disease.

body.p: A health system includes all the people, organisations and resources that deliver health care: community health workers, clinics, hospitals, medicines, financing, information and leadership. Universal health coverage means everyone can get the services they need without financial hardship.

Primary health care, close to where people live, handles most needs: maternal and child health, immunisation, family planning, treatment of common illnesses and chronic-disease follow-up. Community health workers extend it to homes and villages, and referral links connect it to hospitals.

list: Health education: clear, culturally appropriate messages through schools, radio, social media and community leaders.
Healthy policies: taxes on tobacco and sugary drinks, smoke-free public places, food labelling.
Supportive environments: safe places to walk and play, clean markets, workplace health programmes.
Community participation: involving people in planning makes programmes trusted and effective.

body.p: Public-health ethics balances individual rights with community protection, for example during quarantine, and gives special attention to fairness: reaching the poorest and most vulnerable groups first.

body.tip: Know where to find trusted information: national health ministries, national public health institutes, Africa CDC and the World Health Organization.
